video_title: The Rise and Fall of the Soviet Union's Workhorse Computer
transcript: In 1946, America's famous ENIAC burst into  prominence as a "gigantic mathematical robot". A "mechanical Einstein" capable of  doing a 100-year job in just two weeks. Two months after the announcement, the Government  Purchasing Commission of the Soviet Union in the   United States reached out to the University of  Pennsylvania for their own "Robot Calculator". The request was never formally answered.  And the Soviet Union started making its   own computers. One of the more widespread  models was the "middle-grade" Ural-series. The Urals were designed to be mass produced and   across all models hundreds were made.  A steady workhorse in universities,   research institutes, and offices. It  also had a shot at being something more. In today's video, we return to the Soviet Union  and trace the story of its first great computer. ## Beginnings Bashir Iskandarovich Rameev was born in May 1918 to a Tatar family in the town of Baymak  in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. His grandfather Zakir Rameev had been a  wealthy gold miner, a patron of the arts,   and even a poet himself publishing under the name  Dardmend (which means "suffering" in Persian). His   father Iskander Rameev studied mining in Germany  and then worked in the local mines as an engineer. As a schoolboy, Rameev also showed  a tendency for engineering. He built   a radio-controlled model train that  attracted attention from the press for   its sophistication. He joined the Moscow  Power Engineering Institute to study. But in 1938, Iskander was arrested as a  political criminal - perhaps because of   his foreign education and father’s liberal  views - and sent to the labor camps. There   he died - in 1943, reportedly ten  days before his scheduled release. Many years afterwards, the Soviet  government recognized the excesses of   the Stalin era and rehabilitated Iskander.  But the repercussions were far-reaching. Because he was now the "son of the  enemy of the people", Rameev had to   leave the institute as a sophomore - unable to  finish his studies. Struggling to find work,   he after some time became a technician at Moscow’s  Central Research Institute of Communications. Then during World War II, he volunteered for  a communications battalion and participated in   the liberation of Kyiv - providing  radio links to soldiers. In 1944,   he was demobilized and worked  briefly at a radio institute. Rameev was a quiet, gentle person of  medium height and slim build. He had a   very low key personality and actively avoided  publicity. Despite his political persecution   and limited formal education, he would go  on to be an incredible computer designer. ## The ATsVM How Rameev first came to be interested  in computers is not too clear. In a biographical section within a book titled  "Pioneers of Soviet Computing", Boris Malinovsky   wrote that in 1947 Rameev heard a BBC radio  broadcast about the ENIAC and was inspired. A colleague of his at the radio  institute that he once worked at   then referred him to Isaak Brook, who  was working on computer technology. Now, it is true that Malinovsky wrote from  first-hand materials and recollections from   Rameev himself. But that the son of the  enemy of the people is somehow listening   to BBC news broadcasts in the Soviet  Union during the peak of the Stalin   era sounds about as likely to me as  ... well ... it's not very likely. Whatever the real story was, Rameev  managed to learn a great deal about   computer developments outside of the  Soviet Union, get in touch with Brook,   and join his laboratory as a design engineer.  The two then worked on an ambitious proposal   for a computer called the Automatic  Electronic Digital Computer or ATsVM. The ATsVM was a digital, general purpose  computer capable of 2,000 operations per second.   The computer had an input/output, two adders,  a multiplier, a divider, storage memory to hold   inputs and intermediate results, and a main  program controller to orchestrate the work. You feed into it a tape with a  sequence of numerical operations   indicating where to get the numbers,  where to put them and what to do them. The controller retrieves those numbers from  memory, moves them to the adders or multipliers   or whatever is needed, retrieves the result,  and so on. The final result is output onto tape. Interestingly, it also had a little mini-computer  inside called an "interpolator" that   essentially serves as a lookup table to  shortcut certain complicated calculations. It was the Soviet Union's first digital computer  proposal. Rameev remembered that while working on   it, he was staying in random rooms around Moscow.  All of his possessions were in three paper bags.   And to keep himself warm, he burned pages out  of a book of legislation from Czarist Russia. ## The STRELA After the War’s end, the Soviet  government formed several groups   to build computer technology. One such group was  the Special Design Bureau No. 245, or SKB-245. Founded in December 1948 to build analog  calculators for rocket and jet design,   SKB-245 hooked up with a factory  and accepted aspects of Rameev's   ATsVM design to form a series  of computers called the STRELA. The chief designer was Yuri Bazilevsky.  Rameev served as deputy designer,   heading the construction of the arithmetic unit   and the magnetic drum storage.  It was a difficult development.   Rameev and Bazilevsky disagreed frequently  and the tubes were extremely unreliable. They worked nights and weekends - racing  against another high-speed digital computer   project called the BESM, headed by a legendary  Soviet computer pioneer named Sergei Lebedev. At the start, the STRELA gained some favor  over the BESM. It won the Stalin Prize in   1954 and was recommended for mass production.  Seven were eventually produced - though no two   units were entirely the same - and delivered  to research institutes and computer centers. Rameev recalled in 1954 when the  first STRELA was installed at the   Institute of Applied Mathematics, a visitor  observing the computer working exclaimed,   "If we could make five to seven such computers,  the Soviet Union would be in great shape!" In the end however, the BESM pulled ahead  due to its faster performance. Once given   access to the special cathode ray storage  tubes that it was earlier deprived of due   to certain political machinations, the  BESM ran at 8,000 to 10,000 operations   per second. It went on to become one  of the better computers in Europe. ## The M-53 Project (Or the Ural-1) After completing the STRELA, Rameev turned  to a new project within SKB-245: the M-53. It would later be named the Ural-1. Ural obviously   a play on the famous mountain range  in Soviet Russia - but also standing   for "Universal Electronic Digital  Machine for Engineering Research". Rameev's goal was to produce a  workhorse universal computer for   many use cases - ranging from artillery  sighting to solving crystallographic   problems - and designed from the  ground up for industrial production. The Ural-1 computer had a magnetic drum working  memory with about 1,024 word capacity plus an   auxiliary memory of 40,000 words. It ran on over  870 vacuum tubes and 3,000 Germanium diodes. To input data and programs, users  used literal 35-millimeter cinema   tape. Programmers punched series of holes  into strips of tape up to 300 meters long,   divided into numbered zones. The strip is then  glued onto a loop and fed into the machine,   which read it with a Germanium photodiode. At just 100 operations per second, it  was a magnitude slower than either the   STRELA or the BESM. But those were  not its peer class. It was more like   a IBM 650 - a smaller cheaper computer  mass-produced for mid-sized businesses. In a 1956 paper presented at the Soviet  Union's first computer conference,   Rameev argued that judging computers by  their raw operation-per-second speed was   misleading because entering new data and programs  constituted larger bottlenecks to productivity. In response, Rameev designed the Ural-1's  data input with extra automation. And to   simplify things for programmers, he and his  team extended the computer's instruction   set. An instruction set refers to all the  "verbs" that a computer can perform on data. Two in particular can be used to repeat a  calculation many times as it moves through   a list of numbers. That kind of reminds me of  a modern for-loop, my trusty go-to back when I   used to program by hand. Rameev wrote that this  for-loop reduced problem-solving time by 20-40%. ## Producing and Deploying the Ural-1 In 1955, the Ural-1 prototype design was completed and transferred to a factory in the  city of Penza within Soviet Russia. Penza is about 400 miles southeast of Moscow,   sitting on the Sura River. Formerly  a Russian fortress on the frontier,   the city developed an industrial flavor  producing machinery, engines, and bicycles. Rameev relocated there as well to  oversee the production and debug issues,   of which there were many. The photodiodes  leaked. The magnetic drum broke down. The man could often be found right  on the factory floor fixing problems. In late 1956, the first Urals-1 passed  their final tests and shipped to various   computer centers across the country.  Whereupon they often immediately   broke down. These computers were quite  sensitive to temperature and humidity. A writer in 1962 recalled that with  one system over the span of a year,   programmers enjoyed about 73% availability - going  an average of 18.5 hours between failures. Tube   failures were especially common. One system in  two years consumed 3,096 tubes and 5,700 diodes. Despite its issues, the Ural-1 was  the first computer made available to   the Soviet people. By the early 1960s,  it operated in over 128 Soviet cities. The second unit was received by the Soviet  Union's Baikonour Cosmodrome spaceport in   Kazakhstan. Setup took many months, but  once up, programmers produced with it   ten specialized programs that automated  ballistics and trajectory calculations. Their experiences led to one of if not  the first textbook on programming to be   published in the Soviet Union: "Programming  for Digital Computing Machine, URAL-1". The Voronezh University enthusiastically  received their Ural-1 in 1959, enabling   new programming classes and more. It played  a significant role in weather prediction,   surveying and mapping, Monte Carlo  algorithms, and quantum physics. Between 1957 and 1961, 183 of these machines  were produced. Separate spinoff designs were   also produced like STANOK, used  as a metal-cutting controller,   or the Pogoda, used to make  monthly weather forecasts. It was also widely exported, with  versions operating in Bulgaria,   East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Norway,  Turkey, Egypt, India, and more. ## The Ural-2 Then in 1957 - as the Ural-1 made its way around  the country - Rameev proposed a second computer   based off much of its hardware work.  This was naturally named the Ural-2. The Ural-2's most significant change was the  inclusion of ferrite core memory. Unlike magnetic   drum memories, these offered random access without  the use of moving parts. It was a big contributor   to the Ural-2's fifty-fold speed boost from  100 operations to 5,000 operations per second. Other upgrades included the inclusion of  floating point arithmetic (the lack of which   had been a sore point with the Ural-1), a new  instruction set, and larger words for the memory. Unveiled in 1959 - note that the Ural-1  was still in production - the Ural-2 was   one of the Soviet Union's three major digital  computers of the era alongside the BESM-II   and the M-20. The production run lasted five  years, and 139 were recorded to have been made. Units first used in Soviet  Russia were then "passed   down" to the rest of the Eastern Bloc.  The Hungarian-American Charles Simonyi   is a software billionaire who worked  on early versions of Microsoft Office. In an oral history of the Computer History Museum,   he recalled in 1964 first seeing the Ural-2 as a  teen and how it inspired him to go into computers: > I visited this machine [a Ural-2 at the  Hungarian Central Statistical Bureau] once and   I was blown away by the grandeur of it. It's  bigger than anything that I've seen before.   It's as big as a 6600 and it  certainly has more lights ... > The tube was sticking out from a unit,  and next to it there was a light that was   indicating the state of the flip-flop,  and the tubes were of course glowing   constantly in a very nice orange color,  and then the little light was blinking. > And if you can think of a thousand  of these in glass cabinets, or rather,   cabinets with a window in the doors ...  as the machine was running the whole room   was flashing in intricate patterns, very  much like the cheap science fiction movie Communist era filmmakers apparently had  a similar thought. The Ural-2 appears   in a 1964 Polish spy thriller  called "Meeting with a Spy".   Polish counter-intelligence agents would  use it to decode the eponymous spy's signals   and catch him - a symbol of the government’s  competence and technological sophistication. ## Going Into Statistics The next computer in the series  pivoted into a brand new space. Rameev had heard about IBM's burgeoning  700-series of computers in the United   States. This diverse family was  the first of the large-scale,   stored-program mainframes that Big  Blue would come to be known for. They invented FORTRAN for it! Don't  know why that excites me so much. Apparently inspired, Rameev in 1958 decided to  steer the next computer - called the Ural-4,   and it is not entirely clear why  they skipped 3 - towards accounting,   statistics, and economic planning.  To do this, he proposed increasing   the external memory and adding support for  an alphanumeric printer and punch cards. It looks identical to the Ural-2, but cost  almost twice as much at 850,000 roubles compared   to 450,000 roubles. This thing was not small. It  had a ridiculous number of components, weighed 15   tons, demanded a room about the size of a tennis  court, and necessitated 18 maintenance staff. But Rameev’s superiors disagreed with his vision  for the Ural-4. They wanted his institute to pivot   to "control" systems. I reckon that meant systems  that guide equipment like machine tools or trains. Rameev pushed back by arguing an interpretation of  the definition of "control" to also mean banking   transactions, construction material information  and other economic activities. I guess it worked. Then in October 1959, the Main Directorate  of the State Committee for Radioelectronics   attempted to transfer a substantial number  of his team to another institute. A raid! Fortunately, Rameev managed to keep most of  his team and deliver the Ural-4. Unfortunately,   only 30 units were ultimately produced - perhaps   because it still used vacuum  tubes in a transistor world. A Ukrainian named Vladimir Ivanovich  Prusov recalled learning programming   on it during the tenth grade. He  called it terrifying and huge,   but cheekily added that its  performance left much to be desired. ## Going Transistors Throughout what we call the  first generation of computers,   the Soviets struggled to  keep up with the Americans. For instance, ferrite core memories  for computers in the US were adopted   as early as 1953. The Soviets didn't do  it until 1958 with the Ural-2 and its ilk. Production numbers, build quality, and  quality of talents were all lacking.   Component shortages were rife and  Soviet-made Input/Output devices,   magnetic drums, and vacuum tubes broke down  at far higher rates than American machines. A 1967 report of a Ural-2 found a mean  time between failures to be about 22.5   hours - most often due to semiconductor  failures inside the power supply. Moreover,   individual Ural-2 computers wildly  varied in reliability - perhaps due   to environmental conditions  as well as build quality. However, I do believe that the Soviet-American  computer gap really opens up with the transistor.   Bell Labs announced the first  point-contact transistor in 1948. The Soviets immediately join the  race to replicate the results,   producing their first point contact transistor  in 1949. A remarkable achievement. But the   Soviets subsequently struggled to  bring devices to mass production. In 1957, American companies made  and sold 28.7 million transistors.   Soviet production that same year was  only about 2 to 2.7 million transistors. Seven years later in 1964, the  Soviets produced 200 million   transistors and the Americans, some  1.36 billion semiconductor devices   (which may include non-transistor  devices, but you get the point). This gap - which stemmed in part from a lack  of sizable commercial market and would never   be closed - plagued the Soviet computer  industry as it attempted to transistorize   its aging vacuum tube computers to  catch up with the United States. ## The Ural Family In June 1961, Rameev began a project to  transistorize the Ural-4, code-named the Ural-14. When the transistorization effort proved  substantial, Rameev decided to expand   the project’s scope to making a whole family of  standardized computers. He believed that multiple   devices can share design elements, achieve  economies of scale in components, and cut costs. At the start, Rameev proposed a line of  five computers from the Urals-11 to 15,   with each befitting a particular use case.  The core Urals-14 and 15 targeted data   processing plus scientific/technical  problem-solving for computer centers. At the other end, you have the basic Urals-11  and 12 targeting data processing for smaller   administrative offices and factory planning  divisions. And then somewhere in between,   you have the Ural-13 computer targeting  real time simulations for laboratories.   To further subdivide, each of the  computer numbers had an A and B variant. Rameev's team also presented a new higher  level programming language called ARMU,   which stands for the "Autocode for the Ural series  of computers". The concept was something like the   portability that the IBM System/360 line would  be known for. Programs written in ARMU can have   their source code be moved to another Ural  machine - where they in theory should work. In May 1963, the Radio-electronics committee's  interdepartmental technical council approved the   five computers' designs and recommended  prioritization of the production of both   the Urals-11 and 14 in 1964-65 to  replace older tube-based computers. While a major step forward, it was only  an endorsement from what is essentially   a technical review council. For production to  actually begin, another higher-level executive   body must back it and assign the country's  other institutes and factories to the project. Rameev and his team waited for that  assignment to be granted by the authorities,   but it never came. Production of the Urals  11 and 14 at Penza finally began in 1965.   A prototype of the Ural-16 would  not be assembled until 1968. ## Software Troubles While hardware production  brought about plenty of troubles,   the software obstacles were just as formidable. As the Soviets were so late in producing  general purpose computers, they were also   late in producing software. Combined with the  country's ongoing educational issues and pull from   other centers like the military, good software  programmers were in constant short supply. The Penza factory had just a few dozen programmers  working on the operating systems, ARMU translator,   service programs, test programs, and even  custom project software. Unsurprisingly,   a few things fell through the cracks - and  it substantially hurt the Ural’s adoption. One East German professor in Dresden  wrote in his memoirs about a Ural-14   delivered to their computing center with  almost no system software and because of   that it sat underused next to a more  useful East German-made Robotron 300. An East German chemical company used American-made  CDC computers for data processing. Then in 1967,   factory management was reshuffled to reinforce  the "leading role of the working class". So in 1968, the new working class management  brought in a good socialist Ural-14 computer to   replace the evil capitalist computers and reorient  with the Soviet Union. Workers quickly realized   that their new Ural had neither an operating  system nor a higher level programming language.   This plus its shoddily-made peripherals  led to the computer being scrapped by 1972. Now, incidents like this were not unique.  Soviet computers were frequently delivered   without software. But it did not  help the Ural series gain favor as   the Communist Party mulled its solution  to the widening Soviet computer gap. ## Unified Computer System By the mid-1960s, the Soviet  Union had dozens of research   institutes and factories producing computers. Earlier incorrectly hostile attitudes towards  cybernetics had been ameliorated. The Soviets   now made it a high priority to computerize  its economy and society. Despite all this,   the Soviet-American computer gap persisted  and by some measures even accelerated. After IBM unveiled the System/360, the  Soviet government also began exploring a   line of different-sized computers sharing  a standardized architecture, components,   and peripherals. It was called the Unified  Computer System series, or ES-EVM or Ryad. Several computers then existed in the Soviet  Union like the BESM series, the M-series,   Minsk, and Dnepr. But only the Ural computers  had attempted a true family of differently   sized machines running similar (though not truly  compatible) architectures and sharing components. So why didn't the Soviets choose the  Urals? The ostensible reason was that   they were too slow at the highest  end - they desired a performance   between 10,000 and 1 million operations per  second. But that was not the only reason. The Ural computers did not have the full  software portability that the System/360   had. The computers can run the same ARMU source  code, but that didn't guarantee that a program   written on one can run just as well on the  another. It was more of a partial portability. Moreover, in the years of 1966 and 1967 when  the committee was deciding what ES-EVM might   actually look like, the Ural line was not yet  complete. The Penza factory was still working   on it. This distraction also explains why  they didn't much participate in the debate. So eventually the committee resolved to build  something completely brand new. And as it did,   it gravitated towards "adopting" (i.e.  copying) the IBM System/360 architecture. The System/360 was by now a few years old  and its software ecosystem already very   mature. Several of its innovations  had already been adopted by other   Soviet computers with one very  large exception: the 8-bit byte. Believe it or not, a byte didn't always mean  eight bits. Soviet computers used either six   or seven bits. The committee realized that  if the ES-EVM did not take on the 8-bit byte,   then their computers would struggle to  communicate with computers in the West. Even in the days of the Iron Curtain, that  was not desirable. But if you decided to   take on the 8-bit byte, then it wasn't  that much more work to go whole hog,   achieve IBM compatibility, and get  the software libraries along with it.   So that was largely how the decision  to clone the IBM System/360 came about. In October that year, Rameev and the only  dissenting member on the committee Glushkov   submitted a letter arguing against this decision  - noting that the System/360 was already then   an older system, that copying it makes it  impossible to include domestic learnings,   and finally that it will "bring the development  of computer technology in our nation to an end". Some time later, Rameev negotiates and champions  an alternative partnership with British ICL and   their System-4, which is similar to the  System/360. The partnership would have   transferred a significant portion of  ICL's technology to the Soviet Union. In the end however, the other countries of  the Eastern Bloc - particularly East Germany,   which had already moved forward with  copying the 360 - decided that it should   stick to what was then a global standard  and not delay any further. So it goes. ## Conclusion Before we end, I have to say that the history  of Soviet computing is a tough one to cover. But it has been greatly aided by  the Russian Virtual Computer Museum,   which has various helpful resources. Regarding the Ural's development, I highly  recommend the 2005 Russian-language book   titled "The Ural family of computers",  by Gennadii S. Smirnov. He worked on   the engineering team and his account is  basically the only inside source available. The announcement and implementation of the Ryad   system or ES-EVM did not immediately  kill the country's other computers. Advanced second generation computers like the  BESM-6, the Minsk, and Ural series continued.   Production of the Belorussian Minsk in particular  kept on going until 1975, with the Minsk-32 being   the most widely produced second-generation  computer in all the Soviet Union. But more resources being directed towards  the ES-EVM meant less available for the old   domestic Soviet computers like the Urals. Growing  competition for programmers delayed the delivery   of the high end Ural-16 until buyers started  cancelling. Only a very small run was delivered. In 1968, Rameev left Penza for Moscow to  lead software development for the ES. He   would spend the rest of his life working  on national computer design projects.   After his leaving, Penza would not  produce another Ural-series computer. Since many older Urals were still being used  in factories and administration offices,   the Penza factory in 1971 secured funding  from the Soviet State Bank to make an   updated version of the Ural-16 called the  Ural-25. It ran on new integrated circuits,   and supported both the ES-EVM  and legacy Ural architectures. Unfortunately the project took  too long. When actual ES-EVM   hardware like the ES-1020 and  ES-1030 began to emerge in 1972,   the State Bank changed its mind on the value  of retaining the old Ural software and ceased   the work. The last gasp of the Ural computer  was snuffed out and it faded into the night.

At just 100 operations per second, it  was a magnitude slower than either the
STRELA or the BESM. But those were  not its peer class. It was more like
a IBM 650 - a smaller cheaper computer  mass-produced for mid-sized businesses.
In a 1956 paper presented at the Soviet  Union's first computer conference,
Rameev argued that judging computers by  their raw operation-per-second speed was
misleading because entering new data and programs  constituted larger bottlenecks to productivity.
In response, Rameev designed the Ural-1's  data input with extra automation. And to
simplify things for programmers, he and his  team extended the computer's instruction
set. An instruction set refers to all the  "verbs" that a computer can perform on data.
Two in particular can be used to repeat a  calculation many times as it moves through
a list of numbers. That kind of reminds me of  a modern for-loop, my trusty go-to back when I
used to program by hand. Rameev wrote that this  for-loop reduced problem-solving time by 20-40%.
## Producing and Deploying the Ural-1 In 1955, the Ural-1 prototype design was completed
and transferred to a factory in the  city of Penza within Soviet Russia.
Penza is about 400 miles southeast of Moscow,
sitting on the Sura River. Formerly  a Russian fortress on the frontier,
the city developed an industrial flavor  producing machinery, engines, and bicycles.
Rameev relocated there as well to  oversee the production and debug issues,
of which there were many. The photodiodes  leaked. The magnetic drum broke down.
The man could often be found right  on the factory floor fixing problems.
In late 1956, the first Urals-1 passed  their final tests and shipped to various
computer centers across the country.  Whereupon they often immediately
broke down. These computers were quite  sensitive to temperature and humidity.
A writer in 1962 recalled that with  one system over the span of a year,
programmers enjoyed about 73% availability - going  an average of 18.5 hours between failures. Tube
failures were especially common. One system in  two years consumed 3,096 tubes and 5,700 diodes.
Despite its issues, the Ural-1 was  the first computer made available to
the Soviet people. By the early 1960s,  it operated in over 128 Soviet cities.
The second unit was received by the Soviet  Union's Baikonour Cosmodrome spaceport in
Kazakhstan. Setup took many months, but  once up, programmers produced with it
ten specialized programs that automated  ballistics and trajectory calculations.
Their experiences led to one of if not  the first textbook on programming to be
published in the Soviet Union: "Programming  for Digital Computing Machine, URAL-1".
The Voronezh University enthusiastically  received their Ural-1 in 1959, enabling
new programming classes and more. It played  a significant role in weather prediction,
surveying and mapping, Monte Carlo  algorithms, and quantum physics.
Between 1957 and 1961, 183 of these machines  were produced. Separate spinoff designs were
also produced like STANOK, used  as a metal-cutting controller,
or the Pogoda, used to make  monthly weather forecasts.
It was also widely exported, with  versions operating in Bulgaria,
East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Norway,  Turkey, Egypt, India, and more.
## The Ural-2
Then in 1957 - as the Ural-1 made its way around  the country - Rameev proposed a second computer
based off much of its hardware work.  This was naturally named the Ural-2.
The Ural-2's most significant change was the  inclusion of ferrite core memory. Unlike magnetic
drum memories, these offered random access without  the use of moving parts. It was a big contributor
to the Ural-2's fifty-fold speed boost from  100 operations to 5,000 operations per second.
Other upgrades included the inclusion of  floating point arithmetic (the lack of which
had been a sore point with the Ural-1), a new  instruction set, and larger words for the memory.
Unveiled in 1959 - note that the Ural-1  was still in production - the Ural-2 was
one of the Soviet Union's three major digital  computers of the era alongside the BESM-II
and the M-20. The production run lasted five  years, and 139 were recorded to have been made.
Units first used in Soviet  Russia were then "passed
down" to the rest of the Eastern Bloc.  The Hungarian-American Charles Simonyi
is a software billionaire who worked  on early versions of Microsoft Office.
In an oral history of the Computer History Museum,
he recalled in 1964 first seeing the Ural-2 as a  teen and how it inspired him to go into computers:
> I visited this machine [a Ural-2 at the  Hungarian Central Statistical Bureau] once and
I was blown away by the grandeur of it. It's  bigger than anything that I've seen before.
It's as big as a 6600 and it  certainly has more lights ...
> The tube was sticking out from a unit,  and next to it there was a light that was
indicating the state of the flip-flop,  and the tubes were of course glowing
constantly in a very nice orange color,  and then the little light was blinking.
> And if you can think of a thousand  of these in glass cabinets, or rather,
cabinets with a window in the doors ...  as the machine was running the whole room
was flashing in intricate patterns, very  much like the cheap science fiction movie
Communist era filmmakers apparently had  a similar thought. The Ural-2 appears
in a 1964 Polish spy thriller  called "Meeting with a Spy".
Polish counter-intelligence agents would  use it to decode the eponymous spy's signals
and catch him - a symbol of the government’s  competence and technological sophistication.
## Going Into Statistics
The next computer in the series  pivoted into a brand new space.
Rameev had heard about IBM's burgeoning  700-series of computers in the United
States. This diverse family was  the first of the large-scale,
stored-program mainframes that Big  Blue would come to be known for.
They invented FORTRAN for it! Don't  know why that excites me so much.
Apparently inspired, Rameev in 1958 decided to  steer the next computer - called the Ural-4,
and it is not entirely clear why  they skipped 3 - towards accounting,
statistics, and economic planning.  To do this, he proposed increasing
the external memory and adding support for  an alphanumeric printer and punch cards.
It looks identical to the Ural-2, but cost  almost twice as much at 850,000 roubles compared
to 450,000 roubles. This thing was not small. It  had a ridiculous number of components, weighed 15
tons, demanded a room about the size of a tennis  court, and necessitated 18 maintenance staff.
But Rameev’s superiors disagreed with his vision  for the Ural-4. They wanted his institute to pivot
to "control" systems. I reckon that meant systems  that guide equipment like machine tools or trains.
Rameev pushed back by arguing an interpretation of  the definition of "control" to also mean banking
transactions, construction material information  and other economic activities. I guess it worked.
Then in October 1959, the Main Directorate  of the State Committee for Radioelectronics
attempted to transfer a substantial number  of his team to another institute. A raid!
Fortunately, Rameev managed to keep most of  his team and deliver the Ural-4. Unfortunately,
only 30 units were ultimately produced - perhaps
because it still used vacuum  tubes in a transistor world.
A Ukrainian named Vladimir Ivanovich  Prusov recalled learning programming
on it during the tenth grade. He  called it terrifying and huge,
but cheekily added that its  performance left much to be desired.
## Going Transistors
Throughout what we call the  first generation of computers,
the Soviets struggled to  keep up with the Americans.
For instance, ferrite core memories  for computers in the US were adopted
as early as 1953. The Soviets didn't do  it until 1958 with the Ural-2 and its ilk.
Production numbers, build quality, and  quality of talents were all lacking.
Component shortages were rife and  Soviet-made Input/Output devices,
magnetic drums, and vacuum tubes broke down  at far higher rates than American machines.
A 1967 report of a Ural-2 found a mean  time between failures to be about 22.5
hours - most often due to semiconductor  failures inside the power supply. Moreover,
individual Ural-2 computers wildly  varied in reliability - perhaps due
to environmental conditions  as well as build quality.
However, I do believe that the Soviet-American  computer gap really opens up with the transistor.
Bell Labs announced the first  point-contact transistor in 1948.
The Soviets immediately join the  race to replicate the results,
producing their first point contact transistor  in 1949. A remarkable achievement. But the
Soviets subsequently struggled to  bring devices to mass production.
In 1957, American companies made  and sold 28.7 million transistors.
Soviet production that same year was  only about 2 to 2.7 million transistors.
Seven years later in 1964, the  Soviets produced 200 million
transistors and the Americans, some  1.36 billion semiconductor devices
(which may include non-transistor  devices, but you get the point).
This gap - which stemmed in part from a lack  of sizable commercial market and would never
be closed - plagued the Soviet computer  industry as it attempted to transistorize
its aging vacuum tube computers to  catch up with the United States.
## The Ural Family
In June 1961, Rameev began a project to  transistorize the Ural-4, code-named the Ural-14.
When the transistorization effort proved  substantial, Rameev decided to expand
the project’s scope to making a whole family of  standardized computers. He believed that multiple
devices can share design elements, achieve  economies of scale in components, and cut costs.
At the start, Rameev proposed a line of  five computers from the Urals-11 to 15,
with each befitting a particular use case.  The core Urals-14 and 15 targeted data
processing plus scientific/technical  problem-solving for computer centers.
At the other end, you have the basic Urals-11  and 12 targeting data processing for smaller
administrative offices and factory planning  divisions. And then somewhere in between,
you have the Ural-13 computer targeting  real time simulations for laboratories.
To further subdivide, each of the  computer numbers had an A and B variant.
Rameev's team also presented a new higher  level programming language called ARMU,
which stands for the "Autocode for the Ural series  of computers". The concept was something like the
portability that the IBM System/360 line would  be known for. Programs written in ARMU can have
their source code be moved to another Ural  machine - where they in theory should work.
In May 1963, the Radio-electronics committee's  interdepartmental technical council approved the
five computers' designs and recommended  prioritization of the production of both
the Urals-11 and 14 in 1964-65 to  replace older tube-based computers.
While a major step forward, it was only  an endorsement from what is essentially
a technical review council. For production to  actually begin, another higher-level executive
body must back it and assign the country's  other institutes and factories to the project.
Rameev and his team waited for that  assignment to be granted by the authorities,
but it never came. Production of the Urals  11 and 14 at Penza finally began in 1965.
A prototype of the Ural-16 would  not be assembled until 1968.
## Software Troubles
While hardware production  brought about plenty of troubles,
the software obstacles were just as formidable.
As the Soviets were so late in producing  general purpose computers, they were also
late in producing software. Combined with the  country's ongoing educational issues and pull from
other centers like the military, good software  programmers were in constant short supply.
The Penza factory had just a few dozen programmers  working on the operating systems, ARMU translator,
service programs, test programs, and even  custom project software. Unsurprisingly,
a few things fell through the cracks - and  it substantially hurt the Ural’s adoption.
One East German professor in Dresden  wrote in his memoirs about a Ural-14
delivered to their computing center with  almost no system software and because of
that it sat underused next to a more  useful East German-made Robotron 300.
An East German chemical company used American-made  CDC computers for data processing. Then in 1967,
factory management was reshuffled to reinforce  the "leading role of the working class".
So in 1968, the new working class management  brought in a good socialist Ural-14 computer to
replace the evil capitalist computers and reorient  with the Soviet Union. Workers quickly realized
that their new Ural had neither an operating  system nor a higher level programming language.
This plus its shoddily-made peripherals  led to the computer being scrapped by 1972.
Now, incidents like this were not unique.  Soviet computers were frequently delivered
without software. But it did not  help the Ural series gain favor as
the Communist Party mulled its solution  to the widening Soviet computer gap.
## Unified Computer System
By the mid-1960s, the Soviet  Union had dozens of research
institutes and factories producing computers.
Earlier incorrectly hostile attitudes towards  cybernetics had been ameliorated. The Soviets
now made it a high priority to computerize  its economy and society. Despite all this,
the Soviet-American computer gap persisted  and by some measures even accelerated.
After IBM unveiled the System/360, the  Soviet government also began exploring a
line of different-sized computers sharing  a standardized architecture, components,
and peripherals. It was called the Unified  Computer System series, or ES-EVM or Ryad.
Several computers then existed in the Soviet  Union like the BESM series, the M-series,
Minsk, and Dnepr. But only the Ural computers  had attempted a true family of differently
sized machines running similar (though not truly  compatible) architectures and sharing components.
So why didn't the Soviets choose the  Urals? The ostensible reason was that
they were too slow at the highest  end - they desired a performance
between 10,000 and 1 million operations per  second. But that was not the only reason.
The Ural computers did not have the full  software portability that the System/360
had. The computers can run the same ARMU source  code, but that didn't guarantee that a program
written on one can run just as well on the  another. It was more of a partial portability.
Moreover, in the years of 1966 and 1967 when  the committee was deciding what ES-EVM might
actually look like, the Ural line was not yet  complete. The Penza factory was still working
on it. This distraction also explains why  they didn't much participate in the debate.
So eventually the committee resolved to build  something completely brand new. And as it did,
it gravitated towards "adopting" (i.e.  copying) the IBM System/360 architecture.
The System/360 was by now a few years old  and its software ecosystem already very
mature. Several of its innovations  had already been adopted by other
Soviet computers with one very  large exception: the 8-bit byte.
Believe it or not, a byte didn't always mean  eight bits. Soviet computers used either six
or seven bits. The committee realized that  if the ES-EVM did not take on the 8-bit byte,
then their computers would struggle to  communicate with computers in the West.
Even in the days of the Iron Curtain, that  was not desirable. But if you decided to
take on the 8-bit byte, then it wasn't  that much more work to go whole hog,
achieve IBM compatibility, and get  the software libraries along with it.
So that was largely how the decision  to clone the IBM System/360 came about.
In October that year, Rameev and the only  dissenting member on the committee Glushkov
submitted a letter arguing against this decision  - noting that the System/360 was already then
an older system, that copying it makes it  impossible to include domestic learnings,
and finally that it will "bring the development  of computer technology in our nation to an end".
Some time later, Rameev negotiates and champions  an alternative partnership with British ICL and
their System-4, which is similar to the  System/360. The partnership would have
transferred a significant portion of  ICL's technology to the Soviet Union.
In the end however, the other countries of  the Eastern Bloc - particularly East Germany,
which had already moved forward with  copying the 360 - decided that it should
stick to what was then a global standard  and not delay any further. So it goes.
## Conclusion
Before we end, I have to say that the history  of Soviet computing is a tough one to cover.
But it has been greatly aided by  the Russian Virtual Computer Museum,
which has various helpful resources.
Regarding the Ural's development, I highly  recommend the 2005 Russian-language book
titled "The Ural family of computers",  by Gennadii S. Smirnov. He worked on
the engineering team and his account is  basically the only inside source available.
The announcement and implementation of the Ryad
system or ES-EVM did not immediately  kill the country's other computers.
Advanced second generation computers like the  BESM-6, the Minsk, and Ural series continued.
Production of the Belorussian Minsk in particular  kept on going until 1975, with the Minsk-32 being
the most widely produced second-generation  computer in all the Soviet Union.
But more resources being directed towards  the ES-EVM meant less available for the old
domestic Soviet computers like the Urals. Growing  competition for programmers delayed the delivery
of the high end Ural-16 until buyers started  cancelling. Only a very small run was delivered.
In 1968, Rameev left Penza for Moscow to  lead software development for the ES. He
would spend the rest of his life working  on national computer design projects.
After his leaving, Penza would not  produce another Ural-series computer.
Since many older Urals were still being used  in factories and administration offices,
the Penza factory in 1971 secured funding  from the Soviet State Bank to make an
updated version of the Ural-16 called the  Ural-25. It ran on new integrated circuits,
and supported both the ES-EVM  and legacy Ural architectures.
Unfortunately the project took  too long. When actual ES-EVM
hardware like the ES-1020 and  ES-1030 began to emerge in 1972,
the State Bank changed its mind on the value  of retaining the old Ural software and ceased
the work. The last gasp of the Ural computer  was snuffed out and it faded into the night.
